profile.reading:
CoreSite's Atlanta suite, marketed as AT1, occupies part of a much older downtown building at 55 Marietta Street, a 21 story tower finished in 1958 that was, briefly, the tallest building in Atlanta. The tower predates the internet era by decades, and its second life as a telecommunications hub grew out of downtown Atlanta's position as a regional hub for long distance carriers in the late twentieth century. Today it functions as what the industry calls a carrier hotel, a single building shared by multiple competing network and colocation operators rather than a purpose built, single tenant data center. CoreSite, a subsidiary of American Tower, leases and operates a 62,000 square foot colocation footprint inside the tower under the AT1 name, offering direct cross connects to AWS Direct Connect, Microsoft Azure ExpressRoute, Google Cloud Interconnect, and Oracle FastConnect, along with its own Open Cloud Exchange peering fabric.

The building itself changed hands in December 2025, when RadiusDC acquired the roughly 403,000 square foot tower from a European family office that had owned it, with Stream Realty Partners continuing as property manager. Trade press coverage of that sale listed the building's other long standing tenants as AT&T, CenturyLink, Cogent Communications, Comcast, Fiberlight, Lumen, Southern Company, Verizon, Windstream, and Zayo, a roster that reflects decades of accumulated carrier presence rather than a single master lease. RadiusDC's stated plan at acquisition was to add roughly 8 megawatts of new utility capacity, bringing the whole building's site capacity to about 18 megawatts, a figure that describes the tower's total electrical service across every tenant, not CoreSite's suite specifically, and for that reason it is not recorded here as CoreSite's own utility figure.

No source found in this research states a critical IT load, standby generator rating, or onsite generation figure for the CoreSite AT1 suite by itself, and CoreSite's own materials describe redundancy options such as N and 2N power paths without publishing a hard megawatt number for this location. Fulton County property records were not consulted directly for this entry and would be the next step for confirming the tower's assessed square footage and ownership record under its new owner. What is documented with reasonable confidence is the building's age, its role as one of the Southeast's older carrier hotels, its December 2025 sale, and CoreSite's 62,000 square foot presence inside it. What is not documented is any large scale build timeline or expansion announcement of the kind seen at newly constructed campuses, since this is an established colocation floor inside a shared historic tower rather than new construction.

profile.research_note: The 18 MW figure RadiusDC announced at acquisition is whole-building capacity across all tenants (AT&T, Lumen, CenturyLink, etc), not CoreSite AT1's own allocation. Do not store as this facility's utility_power_mw. No CoreSite-specific MW figure found on coresite.com spec sheet page (rendered as marketing landing page, not a detailed PDF). Fulton County qPublic parcel search returned 403 on fetch attempt, not completed this pass.
profile.community_note: Downtown Atlanta's carrier hotels at 55 and 56 Marietta Street sit two blocks from Five Points, and their role as regional interconnection points predates most public awareness of data centers as a land use category, so neither building has drawn the zoning fights or community hearings that greenfield campuses elsewhere in this registry have. The December 2025 ownership change was reported in trade press as a real estate transaction rather than a civic event, with no Fulton County incentive package or public hearing identified in this research.

reading.body:
CoreSite AT1 publishes no power consumption figure, making its compute capacity invisible to AI scaling analysis despite occupying 62,000 square feet in downtown Atlanta.

The facility holds six security certifications that qualify it for regulated workloads in finance, payments, and healthcare. SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, ISO 27001, NIST 800-53, PCI DSS, and HIPAA are not AI-specific, but they permit AI training and inference within the compliance boundaries that regulated industries increasingly require. This matters because AI workloads in banking, insurance, and pharmaceuticals must often run in certified environments, and AT1 can host them.

Georgia contains 33 mapped data center facilities in this dataset, but only two publish megawatt figures, totaling 42 MW. AT1 does not report its power draw, so the true installed capacity across the state is unknown. This opacity is the binding problem for understanding whether Georgia's infrastructure can support AI scaling. Floor area alone cannot estimate power demand without a watts-per-square-foot figure the operator has not supplied. AT1 may house significant compute or minimal workload. The dataset cannot distinguish between the two.
